items.stem: Explain the difference between situational and dispositional explanations of obedience.
items.answer: Situational explanations say obedience is caused by features of the situation, such as the presence and status of an authority figure; dispositional explanations say it is caused by personality, such as an authoritarian personality.

items.stem: Arjun, a junior nurse in Jakarta, is told by a senior doctor over the phone to give a patient a dose of medicine that is higher than the maximum on the label. Arjun gives the dose. Suggest one way the hospital could reduce this kind of obedience.

items.stem: Evaluate Milgram’s (1963) study of obedience in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
items.answer: Strength (validity): Signs of extreme tension suggest that participants believed the shocks were real, so their behaviour was genuine rather than role-play. Strength (standardisation): The experimenter used the same four verbal prods, the learner gave the same pre-recorded responses and the shock generator was identical for all 40 participants, so the procedure was highly controlled and replicable. Weakness (ecological validity): Punishing a learner with electric shocks in a laboratory is an unusual task, so obedience in this setting may not reflect obedience in everyday life. Weakness (generalisability): All 40 participants were American men from New Haven, so the results may not apply to women or other cultures. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss whether obedience is best explained by situational rather than individual factors. In your answer, you may refer to ethics and generalisability.
items.answer: Arguments for: 65% of ordinary men gave the maximum 450V shock when ordered by an experimenter in a prestigious setting. Milgram’s variations showed obedience changed with the situation (for example location and proximity). Arguments against: 35% defied the experimenter, showing individual differences. Personality factors such as authoritarianism are linked to obedience. Perry et al. and Baron-Cohen et al. show that individual differences matter in social behaviour. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Describe the procedure of Milgram’s study.
items.answer: A participant and a confederate drew lots (rigged) so the participant became the teacher. The learner was strapped into a chair in another room. The teacher gave word-pair memory tests and was told to give increasingly strong shocks (15V to 450V in 15V steps) for each wrong answer. At 300V the learner pounded on the wall and then stopped responding. If the teacher hesitated, the experimenter used four standard prods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rigged roles; 1 mark shock generator; 1 mark learner responses; 1 mark prods [4]

items.stem: “Milgram’s (1963) study of obedience has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including generalisability in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (ethics): Participants were debriefed, reunited with the unharmed learner, and in a follow-up 84% said they were glad to have taken part. Strength (validity): Signs of extreme tension suggest that participants believed the shocks were real, so their behaviour was genuine rather than role-play. Weakness (generalisability): All 40 participants were American men from New Haven, so the results may not apply to women or other cultures. Weakness (ethics): Participants were deceived about the shocks, experienced severe stress (three had seizures) and the prods made withdrawal difficult, breaking guidelines on protection from harm and the right to withdraw. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Table: Steps completed (out of 15) — Lab coat: 11, 5, 13, 12, 12, 11, 12. Casual clothes: 5, 11, 10, 6, 11, 8, 11. (a) Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study. (b) The participants were people who replied to an advertisement on a community website in Istanbul. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that participants instructed by an experimenter in a lab coat will complete more steps of the task than participants instructed by an experimenter in casual clothes? Use the data in your answer. (d) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) Participants instructed by an experimenter in a lab coat will complete more steps of the task than participants instructed by an experimenter in casual clothes. (b) Volunteer sampling. Weakness: volunteers may share characteristics (for example being more curious or helpful), so the sample is self-selected and may not represent the target population. (c) Mean for lab coat = 10.9 and casual clothes = 8.9; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 8 and 6) and the sample is small (n = 7 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (d) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2] (b) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2] (c) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (d) 1 mark: advantage of the alternative design; 1 mark: problem it causes; 1 mark: applied to this study [3]

items.stem: In an ethical replication in Toronto, 8 participants were instructed by an experimenter in a lab coat and 8 by an experimenter in casual clothes to continue an unpleasant but harmless task. The number of task steps (out of 15) completed before refusing was recorded. Table: Steps completed (out of 15) — Lab coat: 14, 7, 10, 11, 9, 9, 10, 6. Casual clothes: 5, 7, 8, 13, 1, 11, 15, 10. (a) Calculate the range of scores for each condition. (b) The participants were people selected from a full list of residents of Toronto using a random number generator. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it. (c) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results. (d) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) Lab coat: 8; casual clothes: 14. (b) Random sampling. Weakness: random selection does not guarantee a representative sample, especially when the sample is small, and some people may refuse. (c) Use a larger sample with more participants in each condition, so that anomalous individuals have less effect and the results are more reliable and generalisable. items.stem: With reference to Milgram’s (1963) study of obedience, explain one strength relating to reliability.
items.answer: Milgram repeated the procedure in many variations with similar baseline results, and later replications have found comparable obedience levels.

items.stem: With reference to Milgram’s (1963) study of obedience, explain one weakness relating to ecological validity.
items.answer: Punishing a learner with electric shocks in a laboratory is an unusual task, so obedience in this setting may not reflect obedience in everyday life.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ecological validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Plan a field experiment to investigate whether people are more obedient to a teacher than to a fellow student. Your plan must include: how the dependent variable will be measured, ethical issues and the experimental design.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: status of the person giving the instruction; DV: whether the instruction is followed. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Dubai, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that Milgram’s study should not have been carried out? In your answer, you may refer to protection from harm, usefulness and deception.
items.answer: Arguments for: Participants suffered extreme stress, including seizures, and were deceived. The prods undermined the right to withdraw. Arguments against: The findings are important for understanding atrocities such as the Holocaust. Participants were debriefed and most were glad to have taken part. Milgram could not predict the levels of distress. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.
